whyThisMatters: If you can name the trick out loud together, you will spot it faster on your own — whether it shows up in a crewing offer, a payslip, or a reference-check form. Today's riddles use the same patterns HR sees every day.
rememberThis: This month gave these tricks a name — keep using them. STOP before you open an attachment or update a bank detail, VERIFY the sender's exact domain, then REPORT.

discussionPrompts: Ask someone to spot the difference between two similar-looking crewing domains without being told which is fake.
Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up — DOMAIN SPOOFING and CREDENTIAL PHISHING both involve a fake address, but the goal is different.
Ask for a real example from their own inbox that matches one of these terms.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often mix up DOMAIN SPOOFING and CREDENTIAL PHISHING. Both involve a fake sending address, so people pick one when the riddle points to the other. The difference: domain spoofing is about the sender's address being slightly wrong; credential phishing is about the message asking you to type your password or bank details somewhere.

riddles.riddle: I look like a crewing offer email, but my address has one extra word with a hyphen compared to the real one. What trick am I?
I look like your payslip attachment, but "Enable Content" has to be clicked to open me, and I might be a reference form instead. What trick am I?
I ask you to re-enter your password and bank details together through a link, claiming a new payroll system needs it. What trick am I?
I am a text message about updating your bank details for this month's allotment, with a link you've never seen before. What trick am I?
I say the candidate starts Monday and you must open my attachment right now to keep recruitment on schedule. What trick am I?
I am the three-step habit: 1. STOP before you act, 2. VERIFY using a number or portal you already trust, 3. REPORT to the IT Service Desk. What is this rule called?
